articles.author: NextGenRunGames
articles.description:
A browser game can be easy to open and still be hard to understand. In a short playtest, the first minute can reveal whether players see the main action, understand its result, and know what they can try next.
Start a new player at the normal opening state. Let them play without coaching. Note when they make their first meaningful input, when they recognize what happened, and when they reach a decision that changes the next attempt.
The right sequence depends on the game. In Flingkeep, a player grabs an attacker, chooses an angle, and releases it toward the siege. In Spirestorm, a dive and rebound lead into a choice to bank a haul or climb farther. In Line & Lode, the player casts a claw, tunes its pull, and tries to free ore before the chain snaps. Each loop asks the preview to make cause and effect visible quickly.
After the play session, ask:
What did you think the goal was?
What told you that an action had worked or failed?
What did you want to try next?
These questions help distinguish a confusing goal from feedback the player did not notice. Ask after play rather than explaining during the attempt; otherwise the test measures your instructions as much as the game.
Choose the earliest moment that caused confusion. Adjust one part of the experience—such as the timing of a cue, the contrast of a result, or the transition into the next choice—then repeat the same short test. Changing several systems at once makes it harder to learn which adjustment helped.
A browser preview does not need to contain a full campaign. It needs to communicate one honest reason to continue and make the current playable state clear. Our current projects and builds are listed at NextGenRunGames, with each project page describing its status.
Some projects use AI-assisted programming and text plus pre-generated AI-assisted artwork. No AI content is generated during gameplay; individual game pages list the relevant details.
articles.title: A practical first-minute playtest for browser games

articles.author: Ink Digital Studio
articles.description:
For months my AI outputs were mediocre and I blamed the model. Then I realized the problem was my prompts — they were vague, and vague prompts get vague results.
Here's the 4-part structure I now use for almost everything. It's not magic, it's just discipline.
Every serious prompt I write has these four blocks:
ROLE:      who the model should be
CONTEXT:   what it needs to know
TASK:      the exact deliverable
FORMAT:    how the output must be shaped

That's it. Four lines. The difference is that each line removes a specific kind of ambiguity.
ROLE sets vocabulary and judgment. "You are a senior editor" produces different word choices than "You are a marketer." It costs one line and changes the whole tone.
CONTEXT is where most people under-invest. The model can't know your constraints, yo…
articles.title: The 4-line prompt structure that fixed my AI output (after months of garbage)

TeamCity ships a Kotlin DSL that lets teams define build configuration as code. articles.description:
Most people lose hours every week in spreadsheets. Not because Excel is hard, but because they repeat the same manual pattern over and over: open the file, write the same formulas, drag them down, fix the broken references, export, send.
I built a small system that kills that loop. Three steps, no plugins, nothing to install if you already have a spreadsheet.
The single biggest spreadsheet mistake is mixing raw data and formulas in the same block. Then someone pastes new rows and everything breaks.
Fix: keep a Data sheet (raw, untouched) and a Calc sheet (only formulas). When new data arrives, it only ever goes into Data.
Data!A:D     ← raw rows, never edited by hand
Calc!A:D      ← formulas only, references Data!

Why it matters: you can now clear and re-import your data without ever touc…
